papers.title: Sequential rTMS-tACS Neuromodulation Is Associated with Increased Resting-State Theta Activity in Fibromyalgia: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundSequential application of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) and transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) may induce neurophysiological changes within sensorimotor and pain-related networks. However, the resting-state EEG effects of this combined approach in fibromyalgia remain unknown. MethodsIn this exploratory randomized controlled pilot study, 10 adults with fibromyalgia were assigned to active stimulation (n = 5) or a no-stimulation control group (n = 5). Active participants received one or two sessions of 10-Hz rTMS over the left primary motor cortex (1,000 pulses/session), followed by 10 daily sessions of bilateral 10-Hz tACS (1 mA, 20 min). Six-minute eyes-closed resting-state EEG recordings were obtained before and after the intervention or an equivalent control interval. Power spectral density was quantified in the delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands and analyzed using mixed repeated-measures ANOVAs across central-centroparietal and posterior regions of interest. ResultsTheta power increased significantly in the active group but not in controls, yielding significant Time x Group (F(1,8)=8.70, p=.018, p{superscript 2}=.521) and Time x ROI x Group (F(1,8)=5.53, p=.047, p{superscript 2}=.409) interactions. Follow-up analyses showed increased theta power in both central-centroparietal (p=.004) and posterior (p=.012) regions, with a larger increase observed posteriorly. No significant interaction effects were found for delta, alpha, or beta power. ConclusionsSequential motor-cortex rTMS followed by repeated bilateral 10-Hz tACS was associated with increased resting-state theta activity in fibromyalgia. Given the small sample size, post hoc ROI selection, lack of sham stimulation, and absence of component-specific control conditions, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and require replication in adequately powered sham-controlled studies.

papers.title: Generalizable mapping of the Epileptogenic Zone from interictal Intracranial EEG using an implant topology-aware Transformer
papers.abstract: Presurgical localization of the epileptogenic zone remains a central challenge in drug-resistant focal epilepsy. At the same time, the abundant interictal intracranial EEG (iEEG) data routinely acquired during presurgical evaluation remain an underexploited source of localizing information. We developed an iEEG implant topology-aware transformer that combines interictal iEEG features with electrode coordinates to predict resection targets. The model was trained exclusively on three public datasets (n = 476) and tested on cohorts from five independent centers across three countries (n = 216). In patients with favorable surgical outcomes (Engel I; n = 120), the median area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) was 0.71, and the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.92, outperforming interictal spike rate and clinically defined seizure-onset zone baselines in patients with favorable outcomes (P < 0.05 for both AUPRC and AUROC). Patients with unfavorable outcomes (Engel II-IV; n = 96) had lower prediction-resection alignment (median AUPRC, 0.42), and their highest confidence predictions were located farther from resected tissue (P = 0.005). These findings establish a generalizable framework that integrates neural activity and brain topology to identify epileptogenic tissue from interictal recordings, potentially improving surgical success rates and reducing reliance on resource-intensive seizure capture.

papers.title: Auricular Acupuncture for Erythematotelangiectatic Rosacea: Protocol for a Multicenter, Randomized, Participant- and Assessor-Masked, Sham-Controlled Trial
papers.abstract: Background: Persistent facial erythema and episodic flushing are prominent features of erythematotelangiectatic rosacea (ETR). The efficacy of auricular acupuncture (AA) for ETR is uncertain. Methods: This multicenter, randomized, participant- and assessor-masked, sham-controlled superiority trial was designed to enroll 108 adults aged 18 to 50 years with ETR and a baseline Clinician Erythema Assessment (CEA) score of at least 2 at 5 hospitals in China. Participants were allocated 1:1 to AA with semipermanent intradermal needles or visually matched, same-site nonpenetrating sham stimulation. Four auricular points (Shenmen, Sanjiao, Endocrine, and Heart) were treated on alternating ears every 3 days for 6 weeks, with self-pressure 3 times daily. Follow-up was scheduled through week 10. The primary outcome was clinician-rated erythema (CEA score) at week 6. Secondary outcomes comprised other clinician-rated erythema assessments, patient-rated redness, flushing, migraine symptoms, sleep quality, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and adverse events. The primary treatment contrast was planned using baseline-adjusted analysis of covariance with multiple imputation for missing week 6 outcomes. Secondary longitudinal outcomes were planned for exploratory mixed-model analyses. Discussion: The trial was designed to assess the incremental efficacy and tolerability of penetrating auricular needling compared with a matched nonpenetrating procedure. Same-site pressure in both groups may have physiological effects, which should be considered when interpreting the results.

papers.title: Uncertainty-Aware Deep Learning Automates Artifact Correction for Clinical Body Surface Gastric Mapping at Scale
papers.abstract: Body surface gastric mapping (BSGM) enables non-invasive measurement of gastric electrophysiology, but signals are approximately 100 times weaker than cardiac potentials and overlap spectrally with motion artifacts, necessitating labor-intensive manual review that limits clinical scalability. We present an uncertainty-aware deep learning framework to automate artifact correction in high-resolution BSGM. A signal reconstruction network was paired with a parallel uncertainty estimation network, trained on 2,398 multihour, 64-channel recordings from 27 international clinical sites using weak supervision, a physiology-aware loss function, and uncertainty-gated quality control. In an independent cohort of 127 patients, per-patient signal reconstruction error was 29% lower than with the industry-standard Wiener filter (10.3% vs 14.6%; lower in 103 patients), and remained lower when both filters retained identical samples (9.8% vs 14.6%). Amplitude-movement correlation was 23% lower. Changing only the filter raised the rhythm index across the cohort and robustly altered automated clinical phenotyping in 7.1% of patients, mostly by removing dysrhythmic classifications from artifact-affected recordings. Uncertainty-aware deep learning enables reliable automated artifact correction in body surface gastric mapping, improving signal fidelity and enabling scalable clinical interpretation. The system is FDA-cleared (510(k) K252504) and deployed in clinical practice, demonstrating that data-driven artifact correction can meet regulatory requirements for medical devices and reduce dependence on specialist manual review.

papers.title: The EEG-Respiratory Gap: a deep learning biomarker associated with long-term mortality in obstructive sleep apnea
papers.abstract: The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) summarizes respiratory events by frequency, but was not designed to reflect how strongly an individual's brain responds to them. We developed a deep-learning model that estimates AHI from a single EEG channel (AHIbrain), developed using 22,044 polysomnography recordings and validated in an internal test set (r=0.88) and three external test sets (r=0.50-0.62). From AHIbrain, we derived two complementary metrics that characterize the EEG-Respiratory Gap: {Delta}AHIbrain, reflecting whether a patient's AHIbrain is higher or lower than expected for their measured AHI, and AHIbrain,event-free, estimated from epochs without scored respiratory events. Both were associated with sleep macro-, micro-, and epoch-level EEG features, suggesting that this discrepancy is not solely attributable to model error. Among participants free of cardiovascular disease, both metrics were associated with all-cause and non-CVD mortality after adjustment for AHI and clinical risk factors. After accounting for the same covariates, AHIbrain,event-free was also associated with CVD mortality in the highest-versus-lowest quartile comparison. These findings support the EEG-Respiratory Gap as an interpretable EEG-derived measure associated with prognostic information beyond AHI.

papers.title: Hypothesis-Driven Thalamic Stereo-EEG Informs Surgical Therapy for Drug-Resistant Epilepsy: Outcomes in 117 Consecutive Patients
papers.abstract: Objective Thalamic stereoelectroencephalography (SEEG) is used to characterize seizure networks and guide neuromodulation, yet its safety and clinical utility are incompletely characterized. We examined how thalamic SEEG informs surgical therapy. Methods We reviewed 117 consecutive patients who underwent thalamic SEEG at Massachusetts General Hospital (2020-2025), in whom the anterior (ANT), centromedian (CM), or pulvinar (PUL) nucleus was sampled to test a seizure network hypothesis. We assessed complications, targeting accuracy, the effect of thalamic ictal timing on laterality determination and neuromodulation target selection, and seizure outcomes. Results Small hemorrhages were seen on postoperative imaging for 0.3% of leads (4/1507); all were asymptomatic and none involved a thalamic lead. Targeting accuracy for ANT, CM, and PUL was 81.0%, 94.2%, and 100%, respectively. Early bilateral thalamic ictal signals identified bilateral seizure networks with 75.6% sensitivity and 78.1% specificity, rising to 92.6% sensitivity when bitemporal onset was excluded. Among 52 patients planned for thalamic or thalamocortical responsive neurostimulation (RNS), the pre-SEEG target was revised in 34.6%, including in patients whose cortical hypothesis was unchanged. Most cortical seizure-onset zones did not map to a single thalamic nucleus. Among patients treated with thalamic or thalamocortical RNS, those with early thalamic ictal signals had better seizure outcomes than those without (standardized mean difference 1.71, 95% CI 0.77-2.65). Mean primary seizure reduction was 75.0 +/- 31.7% after RNS (seizure freedom 40.4%) and 90.9 +/- 20.6% after resection or laser interstitial thermal therapy (61.8%). Significance Thalamic SEEG has a safety profile similar to that of non-thalamic SEEG, provides patient-specific information that informs neuromodulation strategy and target selection, and identifies an early thalamic ictal signal that is associated with better seizure outcomes. These findings support hypothesis-driven thalamic sampling in the evaluation of drug-resistant epilepsy.

papers.title: Automated Classification of Clinical EEG Reports as Normal or Pathological Using Natural Language Processing: A Multi-Centre Study
papers.abstract: We evaluated automated classification of 6,829 de-identified free-text EEG reports from 33 Polish hospitals, independently rated by three experts. Three NLP models - fine-tuned PolBERT, a TF-IDF support vector classifier (SVC), and CatBoost - were assessed across seven binary and three-class tasks. Reference labels were derived from mean expert scores, majority voting or the Dawid-Skene (D-S) model, with different treatments of uncertain cases. Inter-rater agreement was moderate (Krippendorff's = 0.585) and below intrarater agreement (Cohen's {kappa} = 0.731 - 0.769); D-S skill rankings differed from unweighted intra-rater {kappa} rankings. PolBERT led on six of seven tasks (binary accuracy 0.876 - 0.952), although its advantage over CatBoost on three-class tasks was not significant. On Task 2A, all models exceeded all individual experts (0.762 - 0.774 vs 0.689 - 0.726). Binary accuracy held at two isolated hospitals; on Task 2A, SVC fell from 0.762 to 0.616, while PolBERT reached 0.797. Errors clustered in disputed reports (accuracy 0.663 - 0.771 in intermediate strata). Exploratory zero-shot Qwen3.8-27B achieved binary accuracy of 0.829 - 0.929, below supervised models, and agreed with experts similarly to their mutual agreement ({kappa} = 0.53 - 0.61 vs 0.47 - 0.63), but favoured pathological labels. Automated classification of Polish clinical EEG reports is feasible across centres, with performance comparable to individual experts. Model probabilities were well calibrated (ECE [≤] 0.035), supporting threshold-based triage. Accuracy depends on expert disagreement and the method used to construct reference labels; label aggregation should therefore be part of the task definition.

papers.title: Single-Case Design for Network-based BCI Rehabilitation: Individual Learning Trajectories and Effects of Motor Imagery Timing in Stroke Patients
papers.abstract: Motor imagery (MI) brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) are increasingly investigated for promoting motor recovery after stroke. However, it remains unclear how BCI control improves through repeated training in stroke patients and whether the timing of MI decoding systematically influences this trajectory. To address this question, we implemented a single-case experimental design involving five chronic stroke patients enrolling in a longitudinal electroencephalography MI-BCI training involving their affected hand. Across 18 sessions conducted over six weeks, the onset of a fixed-duration MI decoding window was randomized to occur 1, 2, or 3~s after cue onset according to an alternating-treatments single-case design. Notably, the BCI combined spectral power and functional connectivity features to classify MI states. The MI classification timing had no significant effect on BCI accuracy, fatigue, or spasticity. BCI accuracy increased across training in four of five patients and was accompanied by patient-specific longitudinal changes in local spectral activity and functional connectivity. These convergent trajectories were consistent with acquisition of BCI control, but were not accompanied by clinically meaningful improvement in motor function. Varying the onset of the MI decoding window provided no systematic benefit for BCI control. Instead, differences in neurophysiological trajectories across patients indicate that MI decoding parameters need to be personalized and reassessed throughout the training. Overall, these findings inform more individualized and effective BCI settings for neuromotor stroke rehabilitation.

papers.title: Revisiting the First Night Effect of Polysomnography Using Wearable EEG Headbands in Older Adults with Sleep Disturbances
papers.abstract: Study Objectives: The first night effect (FNE), where sleep is altered during the first night of polysomnography (PSG), may affect the validity of single-night PSG assessments, yet its magnitude relative to habitual sleep is difficult to characterize using repeated PSG alone. We examined FNE during home-based PSG (HPSG) in older adults with sleep disturbances using multi-night wearable EEG headband (HB) recordings. Methods: Fifty-eight community-dwelling adults aged 55-85 years with sleep disturbances completed up to seven nights of HB monitoring, including one night of simultaneous HPSG. Using HB-derived measures, we compared total sleep time (TST), wake after sleep onset (WASO), sleep efficiency (SE), minutes in N3 sleep, and minutes in REM sleep between HPSG and non-HPSG nights via pairwise comparisons and linear mixed-effects models adjusting for age, sex, and race/ethnicity. Results: Sleep differed significantly between HPSG and non-HPSG nights, with roughly 35 minutes longer WASO, 21 minutes less N3 sleep, and 15% lower SE (ps < .001) during HPSG nights. TST and REM sleep did not differ between HPSG and non-HPSG nights. Findings were consistent when separately comparing nights preceding and following HPSG. Conclusions: In older adults with sleep disturbances, a single night of HPSG was associated with greater wake after sleep onset, less N3 sleep, and lower sleep efficiency than other nights measured with wearable EEG, suggesting that one-night PSG may overstate sleep disruption and understate deep sleep. Multi-night wearable EEG monitoring may help assess the representativeness of single-night PSG measurements, thereby improving the accuracy of sleep measurement interpretation.

papers.title: Clinician belief revision after a background electroencephalography biomarker report in a nurse-led first seizure clinic: the PRISTINE study
papers.abstract: Objective: To measure how clinicians in a first seizure clinic revise their recorded probability of a further epileptic seizure on receiving the report of BioEP, an EEG biomarker computed from background activity, and to explore, post hoc, how the report bands relate to the recorded 12-month working diagnosis. Methods: In a prospective single-site belief-updating study, 86 adults with a suspected first seizure formed the analysis set. A consultant nurse for the epilepsies rated the probability of a further epileptic seizure on seven-category and visual analogue scales after clinical review and routine EEG (step 1), and again after the BioEP report (step 2). An independent, experienced clinical nurse specialist for the epilepsies rated the same probabilities from documentation. All care was decided at step 1; step 2 entries were for research only. Five contributory EEGs were outside the BioEP indication; the 81 non-contributory EEGs (the primary analysis population) comprised 48 directional and 33 uncertain baseline assessments. The 12-month endpoint was the consultant nurse's recorded working diagnosis, not independently adjudicated. Results: The consultant nurse changed category in 32/81 patients (40%, 95% CI 29 to 51); revision direction and mean magnitude followed the ordered BioEP report bands. In a post hoc exploratory analysis of 33 patients with an uncertain baseline assessment, 17/18 unsupportive BioEP reports were concordant with a non-epilepsy 12-month working diagnosis. Three supportive reports provided no evidence of a rule-in signal. As an exploratory whole-cohort pathway comparison against the same working diagnosis, routine EEG followed by BioEP classified as positive 18/24 patients with an epilepsy working diagnosis against 4/24 for routine EEG alone, at specificity 63% and 98% respectively. Significance: BioEP report viewing was associated with graded revision of clinicians' recorded beliefs. PRISTINE was not designed to establish diagnostic accuracy, calibration, management effect or patient benefit.
